speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in a recent Defence Committee meeting the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Dick) denied that his Party had made a promise to increase the annual defence budget in Canada by 6 per cent in real terms. In his perplexed mood, the Minister said to me: "Darn it, I hope you will be able to find one that has 6 per cent in it and I would like to get a copy of it".
I hated to see the poor Minister in such a state of amnesia, forgetting what went on during the last election campaign, so I was more than happy to help him out of his fog by supplying him with three separate reports from the election campaign of 1984, each clearly pointing out the 6 per cent commitment made by the Tories. These reports can be found in the Toronto Star of July 31, 1984, the Halifax Chronicle-Herald of August 18, 1984, and the London Free Press of August 6, 1984.
These reports not only clearly state that it was PC defence policy to increase the defence budget by 6 per cent in real terms but also quote Tory MPs as stating that a PC Government would look last at its defence budget for funding of other programs. In true Tory form, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) lifted SI54 million out of the defence budget in November, 1984. In his most recent Budget, he lifted another $200 million out of the Budget. Now, two out of three Budgets have allowed negative growth in the defence budget. This makes a mockery both of the Tories' 6 per cent commitment and of their commitment not to touch the defence budget.
Instead of an 18 per cent real increase in defence spending over the last three years, the Tories have given us less than 2.5 per cent over three years. That can be compared with the average annual increase of 5.4 per cent under the Liberal Government between 1980 and 1984. Clearly the Government shares this selective amnesia-

subsubtopic: ELIGIBILITY OF EX-SERVICE PERSONNEL-SUGGESTED SPECIAL DISPENSATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 15 years ago members of the Canadian Armed Forces and the RCMP became part of the Unemployment Insurance Plan. Over the years they contributed millions of dollars to help make the plan more financially sound. In January of 1986 our Government brought in measures to prevent wealthy retirees from ripping off the plan. Unfortunately, those changes pulled servicemen and servicewomen into the same category. In other words, those who had served our nation in the Armed Forces and the RCMP, many of whom were forced to retire at middle age but determined to find new work, were suddenly unable to benefit properly from the plan they had paid into. Realizing this, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) recently brought forward changes to correct this anomaly once another job had been found. However, upon retirement, when the need is greatest, those people are still being penalized.
The solution is simple. Our Government should acknowledge service to country and make special dispensation. The men and women of the RCMP and Canada's Armed Forces ask for nothing less and demand nothing more.

subsubtopic: NICARAGUA-ACTIVITIES OF CONTRA FORCES FUNDED BY UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, President Reagan's $100 million freedom fighters against Nicaragua have killed a mother after taking her baby, burned 25 houses, and blown up a 14-year old boy. These Contra terrorists continue as much as possible to avoid fighting the Sandinista Army or even attacking guarded power sites or bridges. They find it safer to assassinate unarmed farm workers, school teachers, health workers and children.

March 27, 1987
On the other side, the Sandinista Government has sought peace by releasing two American citizens caught in terrorist activity, delivering weapons or spying. Why does President Reagan continue funding this campaign of terror? The churches of Canada and the United States have urged him to stop. The labour movement has urged him to stop. A huge majority of the UN, including Canada, voted to tell him to stop. When President Reagan visits Canada next weekend, Canadians expect our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to tell him we are sick of the senseless crimes of the Contras. Cut off the dollars to the Contras and stop the war.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: ACQUISITION OF SUBMARINES-MEASURES GOVERNMENT MUST TAKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, our Government is about to overhaul our national defence system and will soon decide whether we should acquire submarines for military defence purposes. The authorities have yet to make a choice between conventional or nuclear propulsion submarines.
Should the Government opt for nuclear propulsion it will have to consider the advisability of such a decision entailing country-wide economic benefits for our shipbuilding industry. Mr. Speaker, our defence experts will have to take into account the skills of the Canadian shipbuilding industry labour force and their amazing adaptation ability should the green light be given to nuclear-powered submarines.
It is imperative that Canadian shipbuilders be soon given indications in that respect. The credibility of their experts does entitle them to this privilege.

subsubtopic: THEATRICAL ACTIVITIES-REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT RECONSIDER ITS BUDGETARY APPROACH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today, on Friday, March 27, all Canadians working in the theatre will join their colleagues throughout the world in celebrating World Theatre Day.
For over 30 years, actors, technicians and playwrights have been marking this occasion.
This year, however, a pall has been cast on the festivities as a result of the cutbacks announced by the Canada Council in its 1987-88 budget for assistance to the theatrical arts in Canada.
Last year, available funding totalled $17,121,000. This year, nearly $1.5 million has been cut.
For the coming fiscal year, the Canada Council will have a little more money to spend on supporting cultural activities in Canada.
Unfortunately, the theatre sector will not benefit from this increase.
Mr. Speaker, with the thousands of actors and actresses, directors and playwrights in this country, I must deplore these cutbacks, and I want to ask the federal Government to reconsider its budget policy and be more open to the needs of the people in the theatre.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR HOLDING OF BOUNDARY PLEBISCITE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the last day of the last Constitutional Conference on Aboriginal Rights comes to a close another deadline is approaching in the Northwest Territories-the Ides of March. The N.W.T. Legislative Assembly passed a watered down resolution to put the question of a boundary agreement to plebiscite. This plebiscite is to be held on May 20 if the Dene and Inuit ratify their overlap agreement reached last May by March 31, this issue being a separate matter altogether. The Dene have since reneged on that overlap agreement, hence no plebiscite.
A great injustice has been committed against the residents of the Northwest Territories by denying them the right to decide their own future. I call upon the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight), through this House, to direct the Commissioner of the Northwest Territories to hold a plebiscite without any conditions.

subsubtopic: ACID RAIN-UNITED STATES PRESIDENT'S PROPOSED ADDRESS TO PARLIAMENT
speechtext:

When the President last addressed this Parliament in 1981 he spoke of acid rain, stressing the need to "control the air and water pollution that respects no borders".
What will he say in 1987 about acid rain, that it is a serious matter which needs attention for the sake of maintaining good

subsubtopic: TOXIC POLLUTION OF GREAT LAKES-PUBLIC EDUCATION PROGRAM ADVOCATED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the respected Royal Society of Canada and the United States National Academy of Sciences have claimed that people living near the Great Lakes have more pollution in their food than anyone else in North America. It is said this is because the lakes are like a sink, with only 1 per cent of the water leaving the lakes in any one year, so that the toxins added to them will simply stay and stay.
This makes urgent the recommendation of the International Joint Commission, in its call for a major program of public education. Frequently we are unintentionally adding to the pollution of the lakes by the products we purchase and consume. Some of us may be part of the problem. We can become part of the solution, and a public education program will help to achieve that.
As for Canada, is it not an embarrassment for us to be in such a hurry to applaud Moscow for promising conditions that we ourselves would not tolerate for one moment?
The Government of Canada must acknowledge the warning that these contradictions provide and not confuse Soviet promises with Soviet reality.

subsubtopic: PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND CRAB FISHERY-DELAY IN GRANTING LICENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon) is dragging his feet once again in granting licences to some 30 crab fishermen on Prince Edward Island. The crab fishery season opens in only two weeks but the fishermen do not know whether they will be getting those licences. They do not know whether they will be able to take part in that fishery this year.

Mr. Speaker, the Soviet's new policy of "glasnost", or openness, poses some puzzling contradictions.
While criticisms of Soviet life can now be read in Pravda, dissidents convicted of criticizing the Soviet Government remain behind prison walls or in special psychiatric hospitals reserved for political prisoners.
The promised release of 140 political prisoners, to be followed by 140 more, was welcome news. However, according to monitoring groups, some 60 dissidents, less than half the promised number, have actually been released. On returning home, they have been subject to harassment, refused residency permits, had their passports confiscated, or informed that they are on parole. Is this how former political prisoners will fit into Gorbachev's new open society?

The Government looked after the protests from the United States because export permits are no longer required. What will the Government do to look after Canadian consumers and independent gasoline retailers who require this allocation of American crude oil products as security against even higher prices from Canada's integrated oil companies?

subtopic: STATEMENT MADE BY HEAD OF U.S. ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION AGENCY
STATEMENT MADE BY HEAD OF U.S. ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION AGENCY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, how can the Minister express even a notion of progress when the head of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Lee Thomas, is reported as talking about scientific uncertainty on the cause and effect of acid rain at this stage of the process?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT MADE BY HEAD OF U.S. ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION AGENCY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is nothing new in Americans speaking about uncertainty on the question. What is new is that we have a very significant commitment by the President of the United States to invest billions of dollars in this issue. We have an agreement with the U.S. to set up a committee to monitor and give guidance in the allocation of that money. The committee will include Canadians so that we can make sure there is an impact upon transboundary emissions. Under the aegis of the U.S. Vice-President we have a major review of state and federal regulatory practices which will affect acid rain-causing emissions. None of that occurred before. All of that occurs now because of the actions of this Government.
It is not yet enough but it is progress, and we intend to continue to make progress against the destruction being wrought upon our environment by acid rain originating in the U.S.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, yesterday was a typical day in the ongoing game of who can catch the Bears, that is the Russian bombers known as Bears which, with some frequency and regularity, test our air defence system in the North Atlantic. speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Dick (Associate Minister of National Defence):
subsubtopic: INTERCEPTION OF SOVIET BOMBER AIRCRAFT OVER NORTH ATLANTIC
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member poses a very good question but unfortunately he does not have all the information. Two Canadian CF-18s scrambled from Gander to intercept Bear aircraft coming in from the north. Those Bear aircraft turned around and went back to the Soviet Union. While our aircraft were so engaged another two Soviet Bear aircraft came up from Cuba along the eastern seaboard and were picked up on radar by an AWACS aircraft. NORAD in North Bay asked for the closest aircraft, which happened to be those in Maine, to scramble and identify those Bear aircraft.

Mr. Speaker, there have been three incidents of interceptions of Soviet Bears in Canadian airspace this year. Two of the three interceptions were made by American interceptor jets. speakeroldname: Mr. Francois Gerin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: JUDGES ACT, FEDERAL COURT ACT, TAX COURT OF CANADA ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the amendments to the Judges Act, the Federal Court Act and the Tax Court of Canada Act provided under Bill C-41 are important in substance though not in form. Time is of the essence, and I want to thank the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) and the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) for agreeing to have the second reading of this Bill today.
The Bill before the House today, Mr. Speaker, deals with several important matters that concern the magistracy. It is an attempt to apply equality and equity to the retirement age of federally appointed judges. The purpose of this Bill is to strengthen the fundamental principle of the independence of our magistrature, as reflected in the criteria for tenure of office. For the benefit of the House, I will deal with these amendments in the order in which they appear in the Bill.
First of all, Bill C-41 will maintain the indexation of judges' salaries, substituting the Industrial Aggregate for the Industrial Composite.
Under the provisions of Section 100 of the Constitution Act, Parliament sets and pays the salaries, allowances and pensions of judges appointed under Section 96, and thus of all federally-appointed judges.
March 27, 1987

Since 1981, judges' salaries have been indexed on April 1 of each year, using one of the two following percentages, whichever is less: the difference in the Industrial Composite or 7 per cent. An indexation formula was adopted to allow for annual increments so that the Parliament of Canada would not have to make these changes.
Statistics Canada has now dropped the Industrial Composite, and like other users I am asking Parliament to approve substitution of the Industrial Aggregate in its place.
Hon. Members of this House will no doubt recall that for the past few months we have been considering some statutes which were similarly amended, that is the Canada Pension Plan, the Salaries Act, the Senate and House of Commons Act.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, and that is perhaps the most important aspect, this Bill will set a consistent retirement age for all judges appointed by the federal Government.
Since 1971, there are for retirement purposes two groups of judges: those who retire at 70 years of age and those who retire at 75 years of age. Judges of county and district courts as well as those of the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court leave their office at 70 years of age. Judges of Provincial Superior Courts are bound, under the Constitution, to retire at 75 years of age. Judges of the Territorial Supreme Courts and the Supreme Court of Canada are allowed under the legislation to carry on their duties up to that age. In addition, all judges of county and district courts who held an office on October 6, 1971 and judges of the former Exchequer Court which held their office when that court was called the Federal Court of Canada have been given a special privilege. Although the other judges sitting in those Courts will retire at 70 years of age, those who held an office on the date when the 1971 clause was enforced will not be compelled to retire before 75 years of age. Consequently, there are not only two categories of judges dependent on the court, but in some cases two categories of judges within the same court.
When the clause dealing with both ages of retirement was implemented in 1971, the validity of the legislation was never questioned. However, what was valid at the time is no longer so because of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Charter Section 15 did constitute one of the sound arguments to contest these two retirement ages for Federal Court judges. In 1985, in the case of Mr. Justice Addy, the ruling was that Federal Court Act Sub-section 8(2) did prejudice his rights to equal treatment. Indeed it was stated that the law had created two categories of judges in that court, namely those who had been judges of the Exchequer Court of Canada and who were allowed to retire at age 75, and those who had not been with the Federal Court in its early days but who had been appointed later and had to retire at age 70.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) and his predecessor agreed to be bound by the court ruling in this case, to the extent that it applied to Federal Court judges. We have agreed to introduce the necessary legislative amendments so that
Judges Act, Federal Court Act, Tax Court of Canada Act
judges of other courts in a similar situation will benefit from this ruling. The amendments are deemed to have come into force on April 17, 1985, the day when Charter Section 15 came into force. This Bill honours our commitments and sets the same retirement age for all federally appointed judges. We are therefore standardizing the age of retirement to conform generally to the Constitution, and more specifically to the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
To protect the rights of judges who are now obliged to retire at 70 and who may wish to take advantage of the previous system, they will be allowed to retire earlier and will be given the option of retiring at 70 or at 75.
Changing the age of retirement to 75 for the entire federal magistrature will require consequential amendments to the provisions of the Judges Act for election of supernumerary status. The Supernumerary Judges Program allows judges who have held judicial office for many years to take on a reduced workload, without any reduction in salary, provided they meet certain legal requirements as to age and the number of years they have held judicial office.
Election of supernumerary status vacates a seat in the court which can then be filled through a new appointment, while the court can still call on the services of a judge with many years of experience. Court judges whose retirement age is set at 75 are allowed to elect supernumerary status at 65, provided they have held judicial office for at least 15 years, and at 70, if they have held judicial office for at least 10 years.
Judges who are supposed to retire at 70 were offered only the first option, that of electing at 65 after 15 years in office. Now that the age of retirement has been changed, all federally appointed judges will have the same options for electing supernumerary status.
Finally, there are a number of amendments relating to tenure of office. All federally appointed judges hold office during good behaviour. However, they are removable for good reason, under certain conditions. Judges of the provincial superior courts may be removed by the Governor General on address of the Senate and the House of Commons to the Crown. The same statutory guarantee with respect to tenure applies to judges of the Supreme Court of Canada and the Federal Court. Similarly, judges of the Tax Court of Canada may be removed on address of the Senate and the House of Commons, but by the Governor in Council, not the Governor General. This distinction may not seem very important for practical purposes and in the light of present day constitutional law, but it does not provide the same guarantees enjoyed by judges of the courts mentioned earlier. The difference is most flagrant when we look at judges of county courts and district courts who may be removed by the Governor in Council on recommendation of the Minister of Justice.
We believe that, as a guarantee of the independence of the magistrature, this is not satisfactory and that all federally appointed judges should be on equal footing. The purpose of this Bill is therefore to amend the Judges Act and the Tax

March 27, 1987
Judges Act, Federal Court Act, Tax Court of Canada Act
Court of Canada Act in order to remove these two anomalies and provide judges in the county courts, district courts and the Tax Court of Canada the same guarantees for tenure enjoyed by judges of the provincial superior courts under the Constitution.
Mr. Speaker, the last three amendments I mentioned are in response to concerns based on the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. The Parliament and the people of Canada have placed a heavy burden on the courts. We have entrusted them with the task to safeguard our individual rights and freedoms. We expect them to strike a balance between our rights and those of the community, between our rights and our obligations to Canadian society.
It would be strange indeed if conditions for the tenure of judges who are asked to shoulder such major responsibilities were to become a subject for concern, in terms of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. These amendments are aimed at giving judges fair and equitable conditions of tenure, and that is why I urge Hon. Members to adopt this Bill as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to participate in the debate on Bill C-41, an Act to amend the Judges Act, the Federal Court Act and the Tax Court of Canada Act. The essential thrust of this Bill has already been outlined by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Gerin). 1 will not elaborate on the details of the Bill. The Bill makes some important changes of a technical nature which, nevertheless, are overdue. For that reason we are certainly prepared to support the Bill before the House. The amendments in question relate to uniform mandatory retirement age, supernumerary status for judges, and tenure for federally appointed judges. There is also an amendment with respect to indexation.
The age of retirement has been established at 75 for Superior Court judges. This Bill would set the age of retirement for Federal Court judges, Tax Court of Canada judges, and county and district court judges at the same age and establish the same mechanism for the removal of those judges. With regard to district and county court judges, only in the
Provinces of Ontario, British Columbia and Nova Scotia do county or district courts now exist. In all other provinces the superior court is the sole court at that level.
I would like to take this opportunity to raise a couple of concerns with respect to the nature and substance of the process of the appointment of judges in Canada. In November of 1984 the then Minister of Justice, the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), announced with great fanfare that a longstanding dispute between the Government of Saskatchewan and the federal Government concerning appointments to the Superior Court of Saskatchewan had been resolved. Members of the House will recall that there had been considerable debate and controversy about the lack of consultation with the Government of Saskatchewan, and in particular the Attorney General of Saskatchewan, prior to the the appointment of individuals who fill Superior Court judgeships in that province.
In November of 1984 the then Minister of Justice promised a new era of consultation with the provinces before superior court appointments were made. Members on all sides of the House welcomed that promise of consultation. This was particularly appropriate because only a few months previously there had been a significant number of patronage appointments made by the outgoing Liberal Government. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that 23 Liberal Members of Parliament were given public appointments. Of those 23 Liberal Members of Parliament, five were appointed to the judiciary; three to the Federal Court and two to the county courts of Canada. Those five appointments were the subject of considerable controversy.
In the wake of those appointments the Canadian Bar Association established a special committee to study the issue of judicial appointments in Canada. That committee conducted its work from the summer of 1984 until August of 1985. It submitted its report to the annual conference of the Canadian Bar Association in August, 1985.
As I mentioned, shortly after the present Government took office in November, 1984, it announced this new era of consultation. Sadly, while that consultation was announced and there was a tremendous spirit of openness and co-operative federalism, in the case of one of the most recent appointments, the one to fill a vacancy in the Manitoba Court of Appeal, that consultation process was ignored. While we welcomed the announcement of the then Minister of Justice in November, 1984, that there would be effective consultation before appointments were made, unfortunately the Manitoba Attorney General indicated that that consultation was completely lacking in the case of the most recent appointment to the Manitoba Court of Appeal.
Unfortunately, in response to that we have a situation in which the Province of Manitoba has decided to proceed with legislation similar to legislation that was in effect in Saskatchewan prior to the 1984 decision of the Minister of Justice to
March 27, 1987

consult. We are back to a situation where a provincial Government was not consulted and, therefore, will bring forward legislation to ensure that no further vacancies are filled unless that consultation takes place.
Let me return to the Canadian Bar Association recommendations with respect to the judicial appointment process. The Bar Association appointed a committee of distinguished lawyers, chaired by Neil McKelvey, a lawyer from Saint John, New Brunswick. That committee met with many individuals and groups across Canada and submitted to the Canadian Bar Association their report on the appointment of judges in Canada.
The findings of the Canadian Bar Association report on the appointment of judges represent a very damning indictment of the system of the appointment of judges which has existed for many years in Canada.
In their report, the special committee said that Canadians are cynical about the current method of appointing judges and want a totally different approach. They point out as well that in a number of provinces, politics-meaning partisan politics- play too great a role in selecting candidates for the Bench. The committee pointed out, for example, that political favouritism played an especially dominant role in federal appointments to the higher levels of courts in a number of provinces, including New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, and Saskatchewan. They point out as well that with respect to appointments in Alberta, Manitoba, Newfoundland, and in Ontario to county and district courts, political favouritism has in fact been a significant consideration. Indeed, the Canadian Bar Association Committee went so far as to note that in one province 100 per cent of the appointments were to supporters of the Party in power. Obviously there is serious damage to the integrity of the judicial system in Canada when appointments are made exclusively on the basis of one's partisan political background.
The committee noted that since 1978 there was strong evidence to indicate that being a friend of the Party in power in Ottawa and in some of the provinces was in fact the main criterion for landing a judicial appointment. The committee noted further that although the quality of the Canadian judiciary is good, it is uneven, with some of the more manifest weaknesses being attributable to patronage appointments.
