Canagrex

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to speak to Bill C-2, an Act to repeal the Canagrex Act and to dissolve the Crown corporation. The details of this legislation, and the reasons for it, have been fully outlined in this House previously and at the committee stage. Therefore, I will only briefly review the matters involved.
Canagrex has been, in effect, phased out since April of 1985. The purpose of Bill C-2 is to officially dissolve the corporation. As far back as the November, 1984 Economic Statement by the Minister of Finance, the Government has made clear its intention to phase out Canagrex. There were good reasons for this decision.
First, the initiative reflected our policy of fiscal restraint and our firm resolve to make the most efficient use of available resources. Second, it was, and remains, our view that Canagrex was not going to achieve the target set out for it. We believe the industry was not going to use the Crown corporation in the manner planned. Third, we believe that existing government departments would be more effective in co-operating with the private sector in pursuing our trade goals.
Many of the intended purposes of Canagrex were certainly worthy ones. Canagrex was to identify new markets, to promote exports of Canadian products, to participate in state-to-state trading, to provide export counselling to the industry, to make available grants, contributions, loans and loan guarantees, and to import, export, buy and sell. These functions are now being carried out more cost effectively and in a co-operative manner by the Department of External Affairs, the Export Development Corporation and Agriculture Canada. The Agricultural Products Board of Agriculture Canada can also buy and sell, if necessary.
The Export Development Corporation, the EDC, provides insurance, loans and guarantees. Through the EDC, the Government has introduced new, more flexible insurance programs which have succeeded in putting Canada's agricultural exporters in a much better competitive position.
The Department of External Affairs takes a lead role in foreign markets. Its program for export market development will have spent more than $1.2 million for export promotion activities. This program, combined with a promotional projects program, is more effectively mounting Canadian exhibits at international trade shows and bringing foreign buyers to Canada.
Agriculture Canada and External Affairs work jointly on numerous trade initiatives. Recently, the two departments worked to improve their co-operative relationship. The results have been beneficial to agricultural exporters. For example, the two departments have co-operated in numerous technical and promotional activities, seminars and trade fairs. They worked together to develop the export market information system, which provides current, detailed information on

March 27, 1987
Canagrex
agricultural markets throughout the world. They have established a joint committee on agri-food trade. This committee ensures that resources in the two departments are combined, whenever possible, in order to identify new market opportunities, and to help the private sector take advantage of those opportunities. In addition to co-operating with External Affairs, Agriculture Canada works closely with the private sector and the provinces to develop markets for our agricultural products.
Federal and provincial Ministers of Agriculture have reactivated the federal-provincial Market Development Council as a mechanism to enhance market development, both domestic and foreign. The federal-provincial Agriculture Trade Committee continues its active work. These efforts are complemented by Agriculture Canada's Export Expansion Fund and the Export Development of Agriculture Products Program.
The department also provides export counselling and coordinates private sector trade initiatives. Often, the department has been successful in helping to overcome technical barriers to export expansion through, for example, the establishment of animal and plant health agreements with other nations.
The Government recognizes that it is the men and women of the private sector in Canada who export, not governments. The task of government is to assist the private sector in developing and facilitating international trade. It is an approach that is working. I ask Hon. Members to consider the results.
Thanks to some enterprising Canadian engineering firms and officials at Agriculture Canada, a number of foreign buyers have made trial purchases of Canadian agricultural and food processing machinery. Further sales could pave the way for greater economic diversification of Canada's agriculture sector.
Producers in the Maritimes have found new customers for their hay, particularly as a feed for racehorses in the United Kingdom and in the United States. This success story is a result of federal and provincial co-operation with the private sector, as well as support from the federal Export Expansion Fund.
These examples demonstrate that in a challenging world trading environment we are succeeding in creating new export opportunities for Canadian agriculture. We are doing so by creating a positive environment for exporters, by strengthening interdepartmental co-operation, and by forming closer working relations with the private sector. We are proving that we can attain our goals without necessarily creating new corporations, agencies or bureaucracies.
Clearly, the 1984 decision to dissolve Canagrex has proven to be a sound, responsible initiative. I urge all Members in the House to support the Bill that is before us.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, the debate we are participating in this afternoon is really a form of memorial service for Canagrex. The Government dissolved Canagrex well over a year-and-one-half ago. We are now finally completing the formalities of a legislative burial for this agency. I was hoping that the Government might at least have the decency to provide a proper burial. Instead, the description we heard in the statement made by the Government's spokesperson seemed to miss the whole point. What we had was a recitation of the original intentions of the Government in getting rid of Canagrex.
I ask Hon. Members to listen to what they were. First and foremost was a demonstration of the Government's commitment to fiscal restraint. Mr. Speaker, if 6,000 farmers were in arrears with the Farm Credit Corporation, if export markets to Third World countries had dropped by 20 per cent or 30 per cent, and if western farmers and those in Ontario and Quebec were losing markets daily to the European Economic Community and the United States because of their aggressive, massive subsidization of agriculture, do you think you would have brought forward fiscal restraint as your first objective? Do Hon. Members not think that the Government might have at least had the wit to say that, unquestionably, the overriding priority, at a time when the Canadian agricultural economy is facing the most severe challenge since the Depression, is to help the farmers? Would it not have had the wit to say that it wants to help develop new markets and develop new products? Would it not have had the wit to say that it wanted to help farmers develop the capacity to break into areas in which there was intense competition? Oh no, the answer was, "fiscal restraint". Unfortunately, that is the continuing motivation that drives the Government's economic policy, something which is totally oblivious to the circumstances surrounding it, and in many cases the tragedy surrounding it. I cannot believe that any Member in the House would be foolhardy enough to try to argue that, in fact, there is not an incredible crisis facing Canadian agriculture today.
One of the tragedies which I think we have to recognize in this memorial service late on a Friday afternoon is that Canagrex might have provided one of the effective responses to that crisis. Canagrex was specifically set up to provide Canadian agriculture with an alternative means of selling its products, of developing its products and of promoting its products. When the Hon. Member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Wilson) said there was no acceptable proof that it was doing its job, the fact is that in the first nine months of its operation, while the Party of which I am a member was still the Government and Canagrex was in an embryonic stage, it had already something close to $16 million worth of committed sales and was in the process of negotiating another $150 million worth of sales. That is clear proof that in a short nine-month period there was an incredible opportunity of which to be taken advantage. In fact, a vacuum needed to be filled by an agency that would be able to help small farmers, in particular, farmers who did not have large marketing agencies such as the Wheat Board working for them. In a short period
March 27, 1987

of time it was able to develop a sure commitment for $16 million worth of sales and $150 million worth of pending orders. Clearly, that demonstrates the need for such an operation.
The government spokesman went on to say that he did not think it was necessary because there were other departments that could do the job. He referred to External Affairs, the Department of Agriculture and the Export Development Corporation.
I would now like to recite to Hon. Members the events that have occurred since then. Has there been one single additional contribution from the Export Development Corporation to promote agricultural exports? It has had its budget cut back. The only area in which the Government has increased funding for the promotion and marketing of our exports is in the area of defence. The primary objective of the Government is to become a big arms exporter. That is where it is putting its money. That is the area in which it has increased financing, that is, to sell arms overseas, not to help farmers sell their products. When we look at the budgets in the last Estimates the only increase that we can see is with respect to DIPP, the Defence Industry Productivity Program. It received a big increase in funds. If we look at the Export Development Corporation's own estimates we see that there was a substantial reduction.
We admit that other departments did not like Canagrex. External Affairs saw it as a turf battle. It wanted to be the great chieftain of export management and trade. They were to manage this new trade strategy of the Government, and we have seen how they have managed it. The softwood lumber case is costing the Canadian industry $600 million. There have been more countervail cases in the last two years than in the last 20 years. There has been a total and complete withdrawal from any serious commitment to multilateral trade negotiations. They have closed embassies. They have closed consulates. They have cut back staff and financing to the Department of External Affairs. It was to be the great engine of motivation for increasing Canadian trade. However, we have seen a shrinkage, an erosion, a cut-back, and a withdrawal from any kind of commitment.
The Hon. Member also gave us some examples. He indicated that there was a little more hay from the Maritimes being sold to Great Britain. I apologize that I did not leap to my feet and click my heels in wild exultation at that good news. Did the Hon. Member talk about the number of lost sales of specialty crops in western Canada? We have been pushed out of business in the Middle East. Did the Hon. Member talk about losing the opportunity to put together co-op efforts for field crops across Canada. He did not say a word about lost opportunities or lost sales. He talked about selling a little more hay to Great Britain. It seems that is the sum total of the contribution of the Tory agricultural trade strategy.
Canagrex
Although I do not want to strain Your Honour's generosity,
I am tempted to speak for a moment about the other side of the trade picture, that is, the trade war in which we are engaged with the European Economic Community and the United States on the question of grain sales. I must take note, for the sake of relevance, of the response which we received this morning from the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark). When he was asked about the resolution passed unanimously in the U.S. Senate authorizing an investigation, of all things, into Canadian agricultural subsidies, he said that he thought it would be a useful lesson for Americans to learn.
Since the inception of the United States Farm Bill, grain prices to Canadian farmers have fallen on the average of 15 per cent to 20 per cent per year. This spring farmers are facing the reality that when they put seed in the ground they will get 50 cents to 60 cents less per bushel than their cost of production, and that is a minimum judgment. Those prices are being driven down by Americans day after day. With their BICEP program they are pushing us out of markets in Algeria, Saudi Arabia, and you name it. They are after our skins.
The flaccid response of the Secretary of State for External Affairs was, "I do not see anything wrong with it. Let the Americans learn a lesson or two". There is no inclination on the part of the Government to go after the United States Senate and the U.S. administration and say, "What the hell do you think you are doing to us? You have a lot of nerve trying to investigate us when you are driving down prices and driving us out of the markets and when you are about to destroy our grain economy".
Where is the Canadian Government's investigation of U.S. subsidies which are putting us out of business? Where is the diplomatic note asking what is going on? Where is the Government's willingness to go to GATT and say that unilateral action on the part of Americans is breaking the trade contract which we signed years ago?
I suppose we should know better than to expect the Secretary of State for External Affairs to have any backbone when it comes to dealing with the Americans. I suppose we should know better by now than to expect the Government to represent Canadian trade interests with any kind of courage or dignity.
The Tories are compelled by that obsessive demand that they must get the free trade deal on the table. They know the political credibility of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is going into the ashcan. The one way they are trying to save it is by signing a cosmetic deal with the Americans. Everything is sacrificed for that deal. Everything is surrendered. Everything is put up for grabs, including Canadian farmers. Do we have the right to expect any more? Surely, when dealing with agricultural products and the plan of action for Canagrex, one would have thought there would have been an effort by External Affairs, Agriculture, or someone else to make a gesture to fill the vacuum. On the contrary, they have in fact ignored the problem.

March 27, 1987
Canagrex
I should like to recount-and I am glad to share the information with other Hon. Members of the House-a tour which members of my caucus and I took to western Canada three weeks ago. We visited the four prairie provinces and met with over 80 groups, many of which were agricultural groups. Time after time we heard a very clear appeal for assistance of all kinds. I think western farmers recognize that they have to deal with a different kind of international market. Many of our former customers are now our competitors. They realize that they will have to shift into wider diversification in crops and get much smarter when it comes to sales, promotion, and marketing. There is a willingness or a receptivity to begin to broaden and diversify the agricultural pitch.
However, at the same time those farm groups said that they were not big enough to do it themselves, particularly in specialty crops and field crops. Those operators are usually smaller ones and do not have the major economic muscle necessary to mount a big promotional campaign.
They also pointed out that the Government of Canada cut back on agricultural research and on the very capacity to help develop new products and new strains. The Government has eliminated Canagrex. It has cut back on the budget of EDC. It does not provide the support for farmers which is absolutely essential if they are to cultivate new markets. The willingness is there. There is interest and there is co-operation. However, what they see is a full-scale retreat.
We know why that is. The Hon. Member for Swift Current-Maple Creek referred to it in the first words of his speech. It is because they are interested in fiscal restraint. That is very dumb economics. If we force people into bankruptcy and force farmers to go broke, there will be fewer taxpayers to help pay future bills. Fiscal restraint is another expression for squeezing the small guy. The entire country will pay the price.
We know that the legislation simply formalizes a ghost. The damage has already been done. If there is any purpose in a memorial service, I hope it is to draw some lessons from the short nine-month life of Canagrex. The Government of Canada has a real responsibility to give the farming community the support it needs to diversify its crops and sell them abroad in a toughening international market.
We want to see some action. We want to see the trade strategy of the Government incorporating agriculture as a major component. We do not want to see it throw up its hands and say that it is waiting for some negotiation down the road, throw a cream puff at the Americans, or say that we will sell more hay to Great Britain. That is hardly a proper epitaph for Canagrex. It is a compounding of the failure to come to grips with the hard reality of the world of international agriculture trade. All I can say is that we live with some hope that some time soon, someone in the Government will come to his or her senses and do something about it.

Mr. Speaker, I rise at third reading stage of this Bill to make what I suppose will be one last speech on Canagrex. Canagrex had a very short life. It was brought to an unseemly end just at the very beginning of its attempt to fulfil a mandate which I felt was one that needed to be fulfilled.
We do have a great need for an agency like Canagrex to act as a facilitator between the producers of farm products and potential markets. Government spokesmen, today and previously, have justified the disposal of this tiny, budding new agency by saying that there exists in various Departments most if not all of the expertise necessary for farmers to pursue markets in other countries for those commodities that are produced in relatively small volumes in Canada.
When we supported this experimental initiative, it was our feeling that it would help numerous producers of small-volume commodities, from honey producers to pea and bean producers to even at times tobacco producers and soybean producers. The list goes on and on. Commodities that have as yet been produced only experimentally to see if they are agronomically suitable to our climate could perhaps have been grown here under economically viable conditions if markets for them had been made available.
I think it is quite clear to anyone who has attempted to market some of these products for which there are no existing national boards that the act of going through the various departments, agencies and branches of Government to attempt to put together a marketing project is so costly and timeconsuming that very few commodity groups have the volume necessary to make it economically viable. Canagrex with its few dozen experts in insurance, finance and intermediary businesses proved that it could do that for these groups. When people from Canagrex made trips to foreign countries with market potential for Canadian agricultural products, they were able to go with briefcases containing six, eight or even 10 commodities that were looking for markets. They could therefore spread the cost of marketing initiatives over that many products. It was a cost-effective and efficient kind of marketing that was made possible with Canagrex. One need only read its first annual report which, I remind the House, the Government attempted to keep from being presented as it should have been presented by law.
To digress for a moment, I would point out that the Progressive Conservative policy on Canagrex is consistent with the rest of its policies. It had always run hot and cold on Canagrex and it has always been quite contradictory. I suppose that is typical of the words "Progressive Conservative", which in themselves are going in two different directions at once. When the Bill was first introduced, we saw the spectacle of the then House Leader, Erik Nielsen, making a speech at first reading stage of the Bill, something which in itself is quite unusual. On December 8, 1981, as reported on page 13834 of Hansard, he said the following:
March 27, 1987

Madam Speaker, we on this side are delighted to give our consent to the introduction of an idea initiated by the Hon. Member for Elgin (Mr. Wise) when he was in office. We in this party express our gratitude to the minister for perpetuating the idea of the hon. member for Elgin in this legislation.
He then pointed out what a successful piece of legislation it was and what a successful future Canagrex would have from the point of view of the Progressive Conservative Party.
The now Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise), who at that time was his Party's critic for agriculture, rose in the House on second reading debate to praise the implementation of Canagrex. The only thing he could find to criticize about it was that Eugene Whelan, the then Minister of Agriculture, was proposing a budget for the new agency of only $14 million to be spread over three years. It was the current Minister of Agriculture's contention that he would have given the agency $60 million over the same period of time and that, had he continued as Minister of Agriculture, he would have made it a very successful, well financed agency.
The debate on second reading stage went on for some time. The current Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) rose to defend the implementation of Canagrex and outlined some proposals that he had for Canagrex that would permit some of his constituents to export veal calves to Israel. He was quite supportive of the program. In fact, all those of the then Official Opposition who spoke were supportive of the Canagrex initiative until it came time for the Hon. Member for Etobicoke Centre, the current Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), to speak. He took great exception to the implementation of an agency that would provide some assistance to farmers in exporting products. He thought that this was an infringement on the export activities of private enterprise which, I point out, was not doing the job anyway. He succeeded in convincing his caucus over the initial enthusiasm of the now Minister of Agriculture and the now Minister of National Health and Welfare that Conservative Members should reverse their position and oppose to the last drop of blood the implementation of Canagrex.
Those Hon. Members who were here at the time will recall the historic and histrionic display of emotions which then occurred in the House of Commons, the likes of which we had not seen before. The bell-ringing incident that went down in history was attached to this Bill. The Bill was stalled in committee stage. We saw the spectacle of having the chairman of the Ontario Soybean Board, Peter Epp, come from southern Ontario with his officials on two separate occasions to give testimony before the Committee on Agriculture, and because of procedural games playing, the then Official Opposition prevented the committee from hearing the testimony of Mr. Epp on not one but on both occasions. That was the emotion that the initiative of the current Minister of Finance generated over the good initial judgment of the now Minister of Agriculture and the now Minister of National Health and Welfare.
Canagrex
I submit that the agency, during its very short life, showed signs of being able to bring these various scattered bits and pieces of trade and commerce, external affairs, agriculture, trade insurance, transportation and other brokerage operations together under one roof where a producer could go for both advice and service. It succeeded despite a very slow start caused by the political heat generated by the Official Opposition during committee and report stages of the legislation. The agency had succeeded in selling some $16 million worth of agricultural products which would not have been sold without it. As well, about $150 million in sales were under negotiation. Anyone involved in marketing knows that you have to initiate deals many months in advance at times. Those sales were just written off when the Minister of Finance stood up to present his budget statement in November of 1984. That was done without consultation with the employees or board of directors of Canagrex, or any of the farm organizations who used Canagrex. It was simply a unilateral decision by a Minister and members of the Government who, during the election campaign, took pride in saying that they would form an open Government that would be democratic and consult with people.
After that initiative was announced, there were certain moves to avoid the rule of Parliament over procedures engaged in by the Government. The Government attempted to avoid the law which required an annual report to be tabled in the House of Commons. That requirement was avoided for several months, but eventually complied with. We brought the debate to a close over that issue and the official death of Canagrex, the final act of which is happening in this debate, was delayed until such time as the Government began to live up to the letter of the law.
We have indicated there was much that could have been done with this agency. The plight of a great many producers of small volume commodities would be much better than it is had the agency remained in operation. It had the expertise and direction to seek out and open up new markets for those producers. It would have been the contact point for a producer or group of producers who wished to initiate such sales, and it had the power to provide all of the services necessary to complete an international sale, including the insurance and transportation arrangements, without jumping around to a multitude of agencies, boards and brokers. Instead, the Government decided to follow the advice of the Minister of Finance, regrettably so, and overrule the initial instincts and, I think, the good judgment of the opposition agriculture critic who supported implementation of Canagrex in its initial stages.
Because I have only four or five minutes left in my time I want to refer very briefly to another action taken by the Minister of Finance which has been extremely harmful to another group of farmers. I am speaking of the first excise tax imposed by the Minister upon tobacco users and the harm done as a result to tobacco producers. That tax increased

March 27, 1987
Canagrex
tobacco taxes by 40 per cent. It raised close to $500 million annually. At the same time the Minister and his colleagues assured tobacco producers there would be some compensation to assist them in adjusting to the reduced demand resulting from this taxation policy. Two years and five months later there is no program. I was in the tobacco-producing region yesterday and the day before listening to the plight of some tobacco farmers. We know that between 600 and 1,000 tobacco farms out of just over 2,000 are now out of business as a result of this program. They have received none of the promised assistance to this point in time.
Just to put it in context I will tell you how little assistance they were hoping to get. They had understood that of the approximately 40 cents extra per package that the Budget put on the price of finished tobacco products, about a nickel would go to an industry restructuring program. Some 18 months of inaction has produced the demise of close to 600 family farms. There is now a rumour about that there may be a program amounting to about $15 million, which is about 1.2 cents per package instead of the promised five cents, or about one-fifth of the original promise. There are still no details on a program, simply more talk.
Before I sit down I want to read into the record some comments of a woman who appeared before the subcommittee on tobacco yesterday. In the context of closing down Canagrex and another agency I think it is fitting, given the demise of a great many of these tobacco farms, to listen to what she had to say. She recalled an incident on November 11 when she did what she usually does with her younger children in gathering them together to talk about what Remembrance Day means. She said she would like to draw to their attention the fact that the freedoms they enjoy in our democracy were brought about at the expense of other people's lives in the two world wars. She said that they, as the people carrying our traditions into the future, have a responsibility to understand the meaning of those deaths and to try to carry some of these ideals forward. She reported that after her little talk, her youngest son Jonathan, 10 years old but quite keen of mind, stopped for a moment and asked a very touching question. He said: "Why don't I have a grampa or great-grampa who fought in any of those wars?" She explained to him that it was perceived during wartime to be very important to the country to have farmers and that the Government, having realized we could not win a war without farmers, ensured that farmers stayed home to produce food for the survival of the country. Since all of his forefathers were farmers, none of them had fought in the wars. He thought for a few moments and then he said, "Mommy, why don't they care now if we lose our farms? Isn't Canada still a country and don't we still need farmers?"
That is the basic question which the Government is avoiding. It cannot avoid it. We still need farmers to be a country. The Progressive Conservatives understood that when they initially supported the concept of Canagrex which would have permitted farmers to get their production into the hands of
consumers around the globe through an agency with the concentrated expertise which Canagrex could have put together. The Government failed to do that. It has failed the people of Canada and, most importantly and regrettably, it has failed the farmers of the country.

Mr. Speaker, I want to make a few brief comments on Bill C-2. This will likely be the final opportunity to speak to this Bill. I say that with a great deal of sadness because I think Canagrex would have done a lot for our farmers. I supported Canagrex when the previous Government brought the Bill to the House to establish the corporation. I supported the then Minister of Agriculture, Mr. Whelan, not because I was a member of his governing Party, but because I thought that the agricultural community needed some expertise and direction in marketing. I also supported it because the potato producers in the Province of Prince Edward Island were totally in support of the Bill. I had met on many occasions from 1980 to 1984 with potato producers and other farmers in my province. They made it quite clear to me that they, as farmers, did not have to be told how to produce a product, that they were quite capable of producing their products very efficiently.
I remember the great debate on Canagrex. In the early stages after the Bill was originally introduced by the former Minister of Agriculture most Members of the then Opposition, including the present Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), thought Canagrex would be a vehicle to aid the agricultural industry. It was not long after the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) spoke in that debate that most of the then opposition Members changed their tune. I remember the bell-ringing incidents, the tactics which the then Opposition used to stall this legislation. I was not very proud of that and I think that after reflection a lot of the members who took part in those tactics were not very proud of their actions either.
I remember that those tactics brought the subject to the minds of the farmers across the country who derive their income from the production of agricultural produce. They had seen the benefits of Canagrex as we in the previous Government had seen them. In order to remember what people were saying at that time I will read into the record a letter from the Prince Edward Island Potato Producers' Association. The letter was addressed to the Member for Malpeque (Mr. Gass), myself as the Member for Egmont, the Member for Hillsborough (Mr. McMillan) who is now the Minister of the Environment, and the then Minister of Veterans Affairs in the former Government, Bennett Campbell. The letter reads:
Dear Sirs:
At a Potato Producers' Association meeting held on January 6, 1983, a motion was passed that we write to our three MPs and Cabinet Minister to again re-iterate our support and desire that Canagrex be passed as quickly as possible.
We, in the Association, feel that this Bill would be of great benefit to the Island potato industry in the area of export. We feel new markets could be created and old ones strengthened by export credit, which we understand is part of this package.
March 27, 1987

On behalf of the potato industry, we hope you can see your way clear to support this legislation. As to some criticism of the bill that Canagrex has the power to enter the market if it so desires to buy and sell product we do not see this as a great threat provided it is only done when it can be shown the private sector cannot survive this service.
Yours truly,
P.E.l. Potato Producers' Ass'n Norman Ramsay, President
I received many letters in 1983 from people who were interested in the agricultural industry in Prince Edward Island. They expressed the same sentiments toward Canagrex as did this letter. There is nothing the Liberal and New Democratic Opposition can do. There are 211 Members on the government side and they are certainly bent on burying Bill C-2 and what is left of Canagrex. There is no question that we have done everything we could. I have spoken on this subject many times. We should remind ourselves of what Canagrex was all about. The Bill is now in its final stage and during the last weeks and months some of us may have lost sight of what Canagrex would have done for our agricultural industry and other industries which could have participated in the program which Canagrex could have offered. Canagrex would have actively assisted export development in this country.
The powers contained in the legislation that was passed gave Canagrex six main purposes. The first was market identification and intelligence. I have been told by shippers that while they know there is a possibility of markets, since they are small shippers they have difficulty developing those markets in foreign countries. Indeed, many of those countries which may need those products have difficulty in providing the Canadian funds required to pay for them and may require a line of credit.
This was one of the difficulties facing our potato exporters. Argentina and other South American countries do not have enough foreign currency and the producers must wait lengthy periods for payment. They see Canagrex as a vehicle which could have helped them by providing loans and guarantees while waiting for their payment for their product. Indeed, Canagrex could have arranged a state-to-state agreement to sell goods and services.
The second thrust of Canagrex is promotion and information services. Trying to develop a new market in a new country is not much different from developing a new market for a new product in our country. There must be a great deal of promotion and education about the product. Canada is known throughout the world for its excellence in quality. We certainly had good inspection regulations to ensure that we deliver the very best quality products to foreign markets.
It is very difficult to create a new market for a new product that is basically unknown. For example, the promotion of generic fishery products in the United States, which the Government abandoned, would have helped our small producers and processors market their fishery products in the United States. The large companies such as National Sea have
Canagrex
marketing outlets in the United States and, in fact, many have their own marketing and distributing facilities there. However, the smaller companies do not have the money to promote their products and the generic promotion program in the fishery would have helped.
Canagrex could have acted as an agent of the Crown in negotiating state-to-state contracts. It could have provided grants and contributions to help accelerate product development and promotion or the provision of needed infrastructure.
In no way was Canagrex given a monopoly in the legislation over any commodity, either in exporting or importing. Its powers could have only been used in conjunction with private trade, to facilitate exports on a state-to-state basis. In other words, it could have helped any of the agencies, but only at their invitation. For instance, if the Canadian Wheat Board wanted help from Canagrex it could have received that help to develop new markets abroad.
In my area the fox trapping industry has revived in the last number of years. Many years ago Prince Edward Island was a world leader in the silver fox industry but, due to changes in style and other factors, the fur industry declined from the late 1930s until its revival in the late 1970s.
There are a number of well organized and efficient fur farmers in my riding. Approximately one month ago the manager of England Fur Farms Limited told me that he had identified a number of markets for fox furs in Finland, Poland and other European countries, as well as an interest in Japan. He said it would require a lot of money to form a group to visit those areas. He inquired where the funds could be obtained in order to help develop that market, and I suggested the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion.
We phoned that Department in Charlottetown, since it had helped the fur industry in the past. They were able to form a partial package and take two fur farmers to Poland. These farmers had great praise for the two departmental officials who accompanied them to Poland, with some of the live animals which they had to put on show.
While the reception was favourable and there is a market in Poland, it is difficult for Poland to provide the Canadian funds in order to develop the market for the furs and live animals. A corporation such as Canagrex could have played a role in assisting this industry. It would have helped the industry and probably some 150 people on Prince Edward Island.
The fur industry is growing because we have some of the best quality furs. Our fur farmers are progressive and have been able to keep up with the latest developments in crossbreeding and new technology in the industry. However, the premium markets cannot necessarily afford to pay the price and Canagrex certainly could have assisted in developing a strategy for the fur industry for Prince Edward Island and Canada.

March 27, 1987
Canagrex
It is not just Prince Edward Island any more. There are a lot of fur farmers in the western provinces and a goodly number of them in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Ontario. Certainly, the demand is there in certain areas, but there is a problem in some parts of the world to get that hard currency in Canadian dollars.
I come back again to the potato producers and what they have been telling me about losing Canagrex and how they feel it would have been helpful to them. I have talked a lot over the years since I came to Parliament about potatoes. I have not talked too much about potatoes this year because, fortunately, it is a supply-demand situation in which we find ourselves. We are very pleased that the price is good for potatoes this year, so 1 am not here harassing the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) or the Minister of Finance to help alleviate a drastic situation in the potato industry.
I must mention, as I did last year and this year, and will continue to mention, the inspection fees. The Government is going ahead with three cents a hundredweight charged for inspection fees this year. By the year 1990, it will be 15 cents a hundredweight. That is very short-sighted. There was a unanimous resolution passed a couple of weeks ago in Prince Edward Island. That resolution was passed by the good Liberal Government in Prince Edward Island and the opposition Members, the few Tories who are left down there. They themselves agreed there should not be potato inspection fees. I am sure the Minister of Agriculture-I do not know about the Minister of Finance-would have received a copy of that. The resolution asks the Government to act expeditiously to abolish those inspection fees which never should have been imposed in the first place. I have always believed, and always will to my grave, as this Bill is going to its grave today, that the inspection is a protection for the consumer and the cost of it should not be put on the backs of the producers.
I want to say that it is a sad day, I think, that we are winding up the debate on third reading of this Bill which would have given a lot of hope to the agricultural community in my province, but it has been given the death knell. It is now going to its final resting place until after the next election when, hopefully, we will be able to revive it. When we get a good government back in power, we will be able to revive Canagrex and some other good programs and policies which this Government has thrown out.
Other speakers have mentioned that Canagrex did not really have a fair chance having been only nine months in operation. The Government continues to throw the baby out with the bathwater and it will pay for that mistake when the next election rolls around.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when many people think about southwestern Ontario it signifies to them automobiles and automobile parts. However, southwestern Ontario is also a major agricultural area. Many people do not realize that more wheat is grown, for example, in southwestern
Ontario than in the entire Province of Manitoba. It is a major producer of corn. Southwestern Ontario, especially the Country of Essex, is also a major source of cash crops such as tomatoes, beans and so on. Not only is agriculture a major source of economic activity in terms of the growing of products, but thousands of people earn their living by working in factories which process agricultural products, particularly cash crops like tomatoes.
In my area we have major plants operated by Green Giant and by Heinz, and I can mention many other companies of that sort, which produce many thousands of jobs for Canadians.
There was a lot of interest in the Canagrex concept in my area and there is a lot of sadness at this point in time because of the way in which this foolish Conservative Government choked off and is killing Canagrex just as it was getting going in a way which could have been very beneficial to the farmers of southwestern Ontario and the thousands of people who work in the companies which process the agricultural products of our region. The concept of Canagrex was that it was going to assist Canadian producers of non-grain commodities with export sales. Assistance to producers would include the promotion, development and enhancement of Canadian agricultural products around the world. Canada is one of the major producers of food. It is one of the few countries which produces enough food so that it can export food to the rest of the world. That does not mean that all the opportunities for export of Canadian food products, both unprocessed and processed, have already been identified or seized.
The previous Liberal Government received advice that there were opportunities for further sales of Canadian agricultural products, both processed and unprocessed, which were being overlooked and missed through not having an organization operating in the way in which Canagrex was intended to operate. It was argued, and there was strong evidence to support the argument, especially when it came to smaller manufacturers of food products and individual farm groups or farmers, that there were opportunities we were not able to take advantage of and, as a result, the potential for incomes from exports for our farmers and food manufacturers and the resultant jobs were being lost. This was the case not only with respect to those countries where there was a market system but also countries which were essentially based on the concept of state trading. These countries had more confidence in deals where there was involvement of the Government of the exporting country. With the killing of Canagrex, these opportunities will be lost. That is why there is tremendous sadness in my area, throughout Ontario and in much of Canada in the agricultural sector. It is a foolish and short sighted action of the Conservative Government in killing the concept of Canagrex.
At the time Canagrex was first proposed, there was concern among certain people and organizations in the agricultural sector that Canagrex was going to supplant and take the place of activities already being carried out by private sector entities.
March 27, 1987

The previous Government went to great lengths, not only to assure people that this would not be the case, but to modify and tailor the Canagrex concept to ensure that Canagrex would help fill gaps and help the Canadian private agricultural sector to take advantage of opportunities which would otherwise be lost if there was no entity in place like Canagrex. Certainly, by the time the Bill was adopted by Parliament, the private sector connected with agriculture largely, although perhaps not entirely, had come to agree with the Government that there was a need for Canagrex, that there was a gap in filling the potential for exports of agricultural products, both processed and unprocessed, and that Canagrex was there not to supplant but to help the private sector. This I think was proven by the fact that outstanding private sector executives were willing to accept appointments to the positions of operating heads of Canagrex. More important, it was proven by the fact that outstanding representatives of the private sector in agriculture, both from producer groups and from some manufacturing companies, were willing to accept appointments to the Board of Canagrex to help direct its work and ensure that it carried out its mandate.
I do not think people of this calibre would have accepted these appointments if they were not convinced that there was a valid role for Canagrex to play, a role which was not being carried out by any other entity or that would not be carried out by any other entity in the future. I am given to understand that at the time that funding for Canagrex was removed by the Government and it was killed de facto pending this legislation there were deals that were about to be put in place, deals which were being booked, that could have brought in some $100 million more in exports of Canadian agricultural products abroad. If that was the case only within the first few months of its existence, imagine what could have been accomplished if, instead of being killed, Canagrex had been supported and encouraged by the Government responding to the responsible voices of agriculture in my region and across the country. That has not happened. The Government has put narrow inward-looking ideology ahead of common sense. It has put narrow, inward-looking ideology ahead of seeking practical opportunities to help Canadian agriculture find new and additional markets outside of the country.
As a result of the passage of this legislation we will see not only sadness expressed on the part of the Canadian agricultural sector but we know that there will be missed opportunities for this sector which would have been to the benefit of the Canadian economy if this Bill had not been presented and if Canagrex had been supported and allowed to flourish and grow.
When the Bill to dissolve Canagrex was first introduced by the Conservatives in September of 1985, they said that resources would be made available to External Affairs to continue the work of Canagrex. It would appear that that has not been the case. We have looked long and hard in the Estimates for External Affairs for 1985, 1986 and 1987. We
Canagrex
find that there are no funds to carry out this so-called commitment. This is just one more broken promise to add to the ever growing and lengthening list of broken promises made by this foolish Conservative Government. The Government said that if Canagrex was dissolved, the money that would otherwise have been spent in support of it would be there and that External Affairs, through its external trade component, would be carrying out its work and nothing would be lost. But the money is not there. The work is not being carried out. Thus the opportunity for better incomes for Canadian farmers and more jobs in food processing for workers in my area is lost.
What else does this failure of the Conservatives to carry out their promise to provide funds through the Estimates for External Affairs to carry on the work of Canagrex in a different form mean? It is further proof that the Government lacks credibility. It is further proof that the Government, in spite of its lip service, is not really committed to agriculture, at least not to the important agricultural sector of my region, as well as to areas like Prince Edward Island. The riding of the Hon. Member for Egmont (Mr. Henderson) comes to mind in this respect. It also means that in the area of trade the Government is showing its foolishness in terms of not wanting to be creative in order to protect and to create overseas markets. This is not only another move to be added to the long list of broken promises. It must also be added to the long list of foolish actions taken by the Government which are hurting the best interests of the country. There was the sell-out of Canada on shakes and shingles. There was the sell-out of Canada on softwood lumber. There was the sell-out of Canada when it came to our dealings with France on the fishery. Added to this black record there is the sell-out of agriculture in my region when it comes to killing the opportunities that were there and which could have been dealt with through the support of Canagrex.
It may be that for the time being the Conservative majority will blindly march into this place to support the Government in terms of carrying out its blind commitment to narrow, inwardlooking ideology in place of common sense and in place of support for Canadian agriculture in general, and, in particular, agriculture in my area. The Bill may well pass. But we will make sure that the farmers and the workers in the food processing sector in the country, in particular those in my region, will not forget this foolish, narrow, inward-looking move. We will make sure that they remember, so that when it comes time to vote in the next election one of the reasons the Government will be thrown out of office and massively defeated will be the way it killed Canagrex before it had a chance to do the job that the farmers and the workers in the food processing plants in my region wanted it to do in their interests.
This foolish Conservative Government has been working against the interests of agriculture in my area, just as it has been working against the interests of the automobile and other manufacturing sectors. The people of my area will not forget. No matter if the Conservatives use their majority to get this

March 27, 1987
Public Service
Bill through the House or do not, the Canadian people, particularly those in my region, will have their say in terms of what they think of this decision when they vote en masse against the Government and throw it out of office after the next election.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Are there questions or comments?

Mr. Speaker, would the Hon. Member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) care to make any comparisons between the Government's action with respect to Canagrex and its apparent flip-flop with respect to the implementation of a national tobacco agency, which is one of the promises it made in the last election campaign? We permitted the Bill to go through the House and yet the agency is still not in place.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am glad my hon. friend reminded me of this matter. This was another promise made to one sector of the agriculture area in southwestern Ontario. If the Conservatives have some good reason to break this promise why do they not come into the House and come clean and say that they will not proceed with it?
Another sacred trust.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: My hon. friend says-was it a secret trust or a sacred trust?
Both.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
It is both secret and sacred. It is a broken one at that. What will members of the Government say to the growers in the area of Delhi and Norfolk County about this promise? That promise is gone; it has been broken. As my hon. friend said, in the closing days of Parliament before the last election special efforts were made to add to our farm marketing law the opportunity to have a marketing agency in that sector.
There are those who would argue that there may be reasons why that is no longer sensible. There are those who would argue instead that now is really the time to have such an agency since that sector is under pressure and it may well need to restructure. But what has happened to it? I ask that in light of the fact that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) is from southern Ontario. He should have been the one standing up in Cabinet pounding on the table saying: "No. Canagrex is a good idea. I know we said that Canagrex should go, but it is a mistake. I want you to listen to the farmers of my area". Where was he? He was silent. Was he asleep or scared? I do not know. But when it came time to speak up for agriculture in my area he was not there.

PROTECTION OF WHISTLEBLOWERS Mr. Alan Redway (York East) moved:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of introducing legislation to protect federal public servants, employees of Crown corporations, employees in businesses regulated by federal law and employees of businesses contracting with the federal government who report, in a written or oral communication, a violation or suspected violation of any law, rule or regulation, or mismanagement, a gross waste of funds, an abuse of authority, or a substantial and specific danger to public health or safety, from being discharged, threatened or otherwise discriminated against with respect to the terms or conditions of his employment unless the employee knows that the report is false and providing that the employee who alleges any such violation, may bring a civil action for appropriate injunctive relief, actual damages or both, within 90 days after the occurrence of the alleged violation.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I appreciate Your Honour's fine reading of the motion before the House. I also appreciate the Hon. Member for Parkdale-High Park (Mr. Witer) having seconded it.
As all Hon. Members of the House know, the motion before us is something which is known to most people as whistleblowers legislation or a proposal for whistleblowers legislation. That type of legislation is aimed at protecting employees who tell the public of improper practices or improper conduct carried out on behalf of their employers. As we all know, it is a
March 27, 1987

very dangerous thing to do. It can cause great problems for employees who have the courage to blow the whistle or to tell the public of problems about which they learn in the course of their employment.
Of course it can result in employees being branded as trouble-makers, as malcontents, or as publicity seekers. However, worse than that, it may well mean that an employee is fired or transferred to some other department or part of the business. He could be demoted, isolated by other employees or by the boss, blacklisted, harassed, or intimidated. There are all sorts of retaliation which takes place when an employee in fact speaks out and reveals something publicly which his or her employer has done that will cause a problem for the public.
The motion is aimed at getting at the problem of protecting employees in such situations. It is not a problem which is unknown to Members of the House, nor is it unknown to you, Mr. Speaker. You are well aware of a variety of cases in which this sort of activity has come to the attention of the public and has raised concern in the public mind.
I suppose the classic cases are those in the United States. I am thinking, first of all, of the Firestone Tire case in 1973 where a senior employee of the company discovered that there were flaws in one type of tire it manufactured. He advised his employer of the fact that he knew there would be problems. In fact, the employer ignored the advice and censured him. Later, as we all know, there were massive problems as a result with tire blow-outs on automobiles in the United States which caused a number of deaths and a number of injuries. There were lawsuits and replacement tires had to be issued by the company. A great deal of money was involved. Most serious of all was the deaths of a number of people resulting from the fact that the particular person who wanted to blow the whistle was unable to do so in an effective way.
Similarly, there was the classic case with asbestos. It has now been documented that since the 1930s workers in asbestos companies were aware of the health hazards caused by asbestos and that in fact it was not made public. There was the case of a medical consultant with an asbestos company who, when he warned about health hazards with asbestos, was actually fired from his employment.
In addition, we are aware of the Hooker Chemical Company and the Hooker Chemical case. That was the company which gave us the Love Canal, the Hyde Park chemical dump, the S-Area chemical dump, and the 102nd Street dump in the Niagara frontier of the United States. The Hooker Chemical Company knew, as a result of its employees, that it was polluting underground water in California through toxic pesticides. However, it kept it quiet until suddenly the Love Canal situation burst on the world and we all became aware of the great health hazards involved.
In Canada there has been a number of cases as well. The ones which come to mind occurred recently, such as the Ad Varma case in Canada Post. This man indicated that he had information and knowledge that millions and millions of
Public Service
Canadian taxpayers' dollars were being wasted in Canada Post by mismanagement or improper management. He made it public, and of course he was fired.
When he was reinstated, the Government which had a hand in reinstating him was accused of political interference. It was accused of political interference in reinstating an employee who was trying to do a public duty and trying to prevent his employer from wasting millions and millions of dollars.
Even more recent was the example in the City of Ottawa. I am referring to John Quigley in the Department of Immigration. Members of the House are familiar with that case. I understand that the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration is investigating the matter.
Mr. Quigley was fired for telling the public-and I understand for in fact telling the Minister-that in order to get rid of the refugee backlog, known criminals were being invited to apply for landed immigrant status because discretionary powers were granted to immigration officials to deal with the situation. Because he blew the whistle in that case by telling the public and the Minister, he was fired by senior officials. We are now into an investigation of the problem by the standing committee.
The problem is not a new one. It has been around for a long time. Of course, the difficulty is what sort of protection there is for this type of individual who has enough courage to get up in public and try to protect the public. There is very little, if any, protection in the law as it now stands. There have been some attempts to correct the situation.
In January 1985 a task force of the Association of Professional Engineers of Ontario recommended that there be legislation to protect professional engineers in such cases. In July 1986, just last year, the Ontario Law Reform Commission called for legislation to protect Ontario civil servants in such cases.
Recently we debated Bill C-229 in the House. It was an Act to amend the Canadian Human Rights Act, the Canada Labour Code, and the Public Service Employment Act, to deal with the whistleblowing situation in the public sector. Of course my motion goes beyond the public sector. It deals with the private sector as well to the extent that it is possible within federal jurisdiction.
In many American states, there is already legislation protecting whistleblowers. There are some forms of whistleblower legislation in the States of California, Connecticut, Illinois, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Ohio, Oregon, Maine, New York and Rhode Island. The courts in the States of California, Connecticut, Indiana, Massachusetts, Michigan, New Hampshire, New Jersey, Oregon, Pennsylvania and West Virginia have banned retaliatory firings in cases of whistleblowers. Unfortunately, we do not have that sort of protection in Canada.

Public Service
All of us in the House have at one time or another called for open Government and for an openness in dealing with public dangers and hazards. Surely that is what this motion is all about. It is about trying to protect the public, and it is inconceivable to me, Mr. Speaker, as I know it is inconceivable to you, that in this day and age, Hon. Members would not want to do everything in their power to protect their constituents. I urge all Hon. Members to support this motion and to see that it passes so that the Government can introduce legislation for the protection of whistleblowers in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I too have a motion before the House on the establishment of whistleblower legislation and I am glad to be able to support this resolution on the same subject. Indeed, I hope it can come to a vote and that the Government will take account of the feelings of the House and will bring in whistleblower legislation in short order.
From the thought I have given the subject and the discussions I have had on it around the country, I have no doubt myself that it is an idea whose time has come. Canadians, as are people in other democracies referred to by the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway), are indignant when they find that a person who, in their opinion, in editorial opinion and in media opinion, is performing a public service has been fired or charged with an offence under Section 114 of the Criminal Code on the grounds of breach of the duties of a public servant.
While the Hon. Member for York East was speaking, I was thinking not of the cases he mentioned which have occurred in other countries nor was I thinking of the Quigley case. I was thinking of the Richard Price case. In that case, a Canadian official, during the term of this Conservative Government, was working in the Department of Indian and Northern Affairs at a time the Minister was reassuring the Indian communities of Canada that no cut-backs were being planned in Indian programs. At that time, Richard Price and his fellow workers had been assigned by the Minister and the Government to prepare cut-backs in the budget for programs of the Department of Indian and Northern Affairs. Mr. Price, who was a highly principled man and a lay clergyman, got in touch with the head of his religious order in British Columbia and had some consultations with him about how he could square his duty under the Criminal Code and his normal master-servant common-law duty, which is also very clearly defined, with his sense that there was a higher public interest to be served by going public.
In this case, Richard Price went public. He gave his information to a Member of Parliament who raised it here in the House of Commons and across the country. The public servant was suspended and charges were laid against him by the Attorney General of Canada. Then there was a big public outcry in this House and elsewhere in which I was involved on behalf of our Party. In the end, the Attorney General backed off and did not proceed with charges.
There is a balance that must be achieved. I have been a Minister of the Crown and I hope to be one again. I would like to see us move on reforms with which we can live. I think the general duty of a public servant to respect his undertakings of confidence and loyalty to his employer, the Government, not the larger sense of the Canadian people at large, must be real. Again, while the Hon. Member for York East was speaking, I was thinking of a situation I experienced which Hon. Members might find enlightening.
While I was Solicitor General, I received a letter from a corporation that owned an island off the coast of Canada, and I will not be any more specific than that. This corporation was closing down an industrial operation on that island and had the idea that it might make a good prison colony. Canada does not have prison colonies. A prison colony is a place where inmates and free people together go to live in a community. There is some measure of surveillance, but the people who are serving time basically act like the other people and interact with the other people. Those who are serving time can hold regular jobs and can live with their families. In other words, it is an interesting idea that has not been part of the Canadian tradition.
I wanted to give the matter some thought. One of the first things I was advised about by my political advisers was the political aspects of the matter. We were worried on the one hand that some Canadians would say we wanted to set up a Siberia in Canada while, on the other hand, others might say that we wanted to set up a paradise island where inmates could live with their families rather than being punished for having committed crimes. I wanted to think my way through the problem, but I also wanted some time to decide what position 1 could take with respect to my colleagues in Cabinet, what position we could advocate.
If, during my consideration of the matter, a member of my Department had felt free to go to the media to reveal the story that the Minister was thinking about establishing a Siberia or thinking about establishing a paradise island for inmates, I would not have been able to respond properly to the idea. That is only one example showing why a balance is needed. There are thousands of examples, some more sensitive than others, proving that a Minister should be able to count on the discretion of his or her officials and should not feel that the officials will go around thinking that while they work for the Government, they also work for the taxpayers and they had better warn the taxpayers about certain things.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for York East, has come up with a pretty good list of exceptions, cases in which officials should feel entitled to go public and to be protected. Obviously a good case is when a crime is being planned or committed. Another good case is when there is a danger to public health, public safety or the environment. As well, it is possible that a Minister could lie in the House, as occurred in the General Belgrano case. In that case, a Minister of the Crown in Great Britain said the reason the armed forces shot the General Belgrano was that it was approaching their theatre of war,
March 27, 1987

while in fact all the records of the department showed that the General Belgrano was leaving the area of conflict and therefore there was no excuse for shooting it. This aggravated the war and resulted in the loss of lives. Such a case, which I am sure my friend would add to his list, would be a good one as well.
Just before I conclude, I want to deal with another dimension of the problem, and that is the sanctions that should be available to the Government for a government employee who improperly blows the whistle. I wonder why the Crown requires the protection of the Criminal Code in so many cases. If an official blows the whistle when he should not have, why does the Government not use the ordinary remedies open to an employer whose employee is in breach of his duties? Why does the Government not simply fire the employee, demote him, dock his pay or put a black mark on his performance record? The sanctions available to the Crown are pretty dramatic. Fourteen years in prison is too great a sanction for an employer to have, even if it is the Government, in order to force employees to toe the line and comply with the duties attached to their employment. I am not saying there are not certain areas where blowing the whistle improperly or going public improperly could cause a disaster. For example, an official giving secrets to a foreign power that would use them against Canada is a good example of where Criminal Code sanctions should apply. However, in this case it is broader than it needs to be. I would like to see a whistleblower law, but not the way some states have it where an official can go public when it is in the "public interest" to do so. That just gives the problem to the courts, and I do not think that is an appropriate way for legislators to deal with the problem.
My third point is that we should have sanctions which are more like those that a normal employer has when an employee steps out of line.

Mr. Speaker, I just wanted to say a few words in support of this resolution. I think the notion of having legislation to cover those people who speak out in the public interest when their organization is doing something wrong, or contrary to the public interest, is an idea whose time has come.
When an organization, whether it be government or private, is threatening people's health or safety, wasting public resources, or breaking the law, people who work for those organizations should have the right to blow the whistle, so to speak, so that the public is informed about what is going on. When I say "blow the whistle", that brings to mind the image of a policeman, a cop. What we are really looking for here is a citizen cop who can make a citizen's arrest when organizations are operating contrary to the public interest. We have had examples in Canada where it would have been worthwhile to have legal protection in place for someone who is willing to speak out. We all know that there is pressure to fall in line, and that includes legal sanctions. It takes a great deal of
Public Service
courage for someone to speak out. If a law is being broken, then someone should be able to speak out about it and be protected when doing so. There was the example of Ad Varma, who worked for the Post Office. He said millions of dollars were being wasted and spoke out about it. He lost his job as a result. The newly-elected Government took another look at that case and decided he had been unfairly treated and should be given his job back. In fact, an investigation was made into his claims. The outcome was not entirely satisfactory in that the report says that the investigators were not really able to determine whether his claims were accurate. Perhaps more facts about that case will come out in the future, who knows?
There have been examples in the auto industry involving safety. People have had knowledge that a car their company produced was unsafe. I remember one gentleman who waited until he retired before he spoke out. He lived for years with this knowledge, and of course people died in the interim. Therefore the time has come to strike a new balance between responsibility to the public and responsibility to the organization you work for.
In the case of Government, obviously there has to be confidentiality in order for Government to function and develop policy. We all have a lot of experience in this city with government documents being leaked, and it does not seem possible for a Government to keep anything confidential. It always ends up in the public arena before the Government wants it there. There has to be a balance between the need for secrecy in Government and the need to provide some protection for those willing to speak out when the public interest has been severely breached. That applies whether it is a law being broken or whether it involves people's health and safety. That is where we need to strike a new balance so that people who are willing to speak out can be given some protection.

Mr. Speaker, I just wish to say that I support this motion, because it is about time we provide protection for employees who have the courage to indicate that their organization is acting in a way that is detrimental to the public interest. It is necessary to balance this protection with the organization's need for confidentiality. Now is the time to find a new balance.
