Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak to this motion I would like to thank the Hon. Member from York East (Mr. Redway) for this expression of his concern for the rights of Canadian workers. I share his concern, and I am eager to support any measure that would improve the safety of Canadian workplaces and the accountability of employers in the federal jurisdiction.
I will limit my comments to the safety and health implications of the motion, for I am very concerned about the appalling losses of life and property caused by industrial accidents. As you may know, Mr. Speaker, every year in this country about 1,000 workers die and many more are seriously injured because of workplace accidents and employment-related illnesses. In addition to the pain and suffering that

March 27, 1987
Public Service
result, these accidents and illnesses take some $14 billion out of the economy in the form of lost wages, lost production, equipment damage, and workers' compensation payments. If the Hon. Member's motion represented even a partial solution to this serious problem I would gladly support it.
Unfortunately, I fear that the action suggested by this motion would not offer such a solution. In fact, it might reduce the efficiency of existing procedures under the Canada Labour Code for preventing potentially hazardous working conditions. It might even create an atmosphere of confrontation and hostility in certain workplaces, which would be both contrary to the goals and policies of this Government and itself a threat to workplace safety.
The Hon. Member's motion is intended to protect workers who resort to a practice known in labour affairs circles as "whistle blowing". The phrase implies that, if an employee knows that his or her employer is engaging in illegal, unscrupulous, or dangerous practices, he or she is not obliged to meekly go along with a course of action that is wrong, but may instead "blow the whistle"-that is, inform the authorities or the general public through the news media and thus help end the abuse.
Certainly, Mr. Speaker, the responsiblity of the law-abiding citizen to defend the public good does supersede the employee's loyalty to an unscrupulous employer.
But there are ways already provided in law for employees to report irregularities without inviting retaliatory action from the employer.
The majority of workers under federal jurisdiction belong to unions, and a union can bring strong pressure to bear on a delinquent employer. In most cases, a concerned worker would be best advised to inform his or her union of any irregularities such as are foreseen in this motion and rely on the established practices of the industrial relations system to correct the matter. The employee who complained would remain anonymous and so need not fear retaliation. Where safety and health are concerned, both unionized and non-unionized workers are protected by provisions of the Canada Labour Code that guarantee the right to refuse dangerous work.
Let me briefly describe what happens under present legislation when an employee believes that his or her employer is in violation of safety and health regulations or engaging in practices that could create, in the Hon. Member's words, "a substantial and specific danger to public health or safety". Section 85 of the Canada Labour Code states that, if an employee has reasonable cause to believe that a particular work process or condition could be dangerous to himself or any other employee, the employee has the right to refuse to do the work, without being subject to any disciplinary action or discriminatory treatment because of the refusal.
In certain cases, these conditions could have public safety implications. For example, a truck driver required to drive in excess of the maximum hours permissible under the Code may pose a threat to employee and public safety. There are
established steps that must be taken when an employee refuses to do dangerous work. First, the employee must inform the employer of the refusal to work and the reasons for it, and also report the incident to the workplace safety and health committee or representative. Second, the employer must then investigate the condition, along with the safety and health representative or a member of the committee. Third, if the condition is not corrected to the employee's satisfaction, a Canada Safety officer is to be called in to investigate the complaint. Fourth, if the employee is still not satisfied that the condition is safe or has been corrected, the matter may be referred to the Canada Labour Relations Board for adjudication.
Throughout this procedure, the employee is protected from dismissal or discriminatory treatment for refusing to work in dangerous conditions. The Canada Labour Relations Board has the authority to make the employer reinstate an employee who has been dismissed for this reason, rescind any disciplinary action, and repay any wages the employee may have lost because of the employer's discriminatory action.
Furthermore, under Section 72 of the Canada Labour Code, an employee who complains to the Minister of Labour about any irregular working conditions imposed by the employer may request that his or her identity be kept secret. Clearly, a worker who chooses, instead, to blow the whistle on his or her employer by reporting abuses to the news media cannot expect to remain anonymous. In short, Mr. Speaker, the intent of the Hon. Member's motion, insofar as it concerns circumstances under the purview of the Canada Labour Code, is already being adequately met by the existing legislation.
Furthermore, the measures recommended in the motion, if adopted by this House, could potentially disrupt the Government's whole approach to ensuring workplace safety and health. This Government takes very seriously its responsibility to improve the safety and health of Canadian workplaces. Over the past year it has implemented a coordinated policy to ensure that employers and employees comply with the occupational safety and health regulations that have been drafted into law.
Fundamental to this compliance policy is the recognition that occupational safety and health is the joint responsibility of employers and employees. Mandatory joint safety and health committees have been established because we believe that, whatever their differences at the bargaining table, employers and employees have a common interest in making their workplaces safer and thus more productive. We do not assume that all employers are angels, and the policy does provide for swift and strong action against an employer when warranted.
But we do give employers credit for acting responsibly in this area of common concern, and we recognize that it is the people who work in an establishment, employers and employees together, who are best able to ensure the safety and health of that establishement. Only an atmosphere of cooperation will help ensure safer workplaces and a less secretive management.
March 27, 1987

The measures proposed in the Hon. Member's motion, on the contrary, would foster an adversarial approach, which I believe is in no one's interest. The potential is there for a few disgruntled employees to make frivolous disclosures inspired by spite rather than commitment to public good, and this could discredit many others whose concerns are well-founded.
Equally dangerous, complex issues involving interpretation of the law might end up being debated in the news media, with all the inaccuracies and confusions that would inevitably result. So, by encouraging public disclosures rather than cooperative problem solving, the procedures recommended in this motion may well result in a hardening of attitudes that would work against a speedy resolution of problems in the workplace.
This could only result in more confrontation, less cooperation, less sharing of information on safety and health matters, and therefore greater secrecy and suspicion and a more dangerous working environment for Canadians.
For all of these reasons I recommend that all Hon. Members reject this well-intentioned but ill-conceived motion.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with a great deal of attention to the remarks of my hon. colleagues on the Bill introduced by the man we call Mr. Redway. I prefer to use his name as we see it here.
Members always say that they did not intend to participate and will not be long, but end up talking extensively. However, I will try to make the shortest speech of my 23-year career.

My hon. colleague, the Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan), has put on the record his views in favour of the motion. I do not wish to repeat what he or the Hon. Member for York East said. 1 favour the Bill. I see nothing wrong with studying it further in committee. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to have participated so briefly. 1 believe that my colleagues, too, should speak briefly and allow the motion to be sent to the appropriate committee for further study, amendment and action.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak concerning motion M-92, proposed by the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway).
Basically, the motion calls upon the Government to consider the advisability of introducing legislation to protect federal public servants, employees of Crown corporations, employees in businesses regulated by the federal Government and employees of businesses contracting with the federal Government from being discharged, threatened or otherwise discriminated against for having reported legal violations, mismanagement or other wrongdoings on the part of their employers. The motion further stipulates that the employee
Public Service
should have the right to bring a civil action for appropriate injunctive relief or damages in cases where he or she is made to suffer for his or her disclosure.
Mr. Speaker, I realize that this motion seeks to achieve a number of desirable goals. At least in its principle in our society, and in an age when many persons distrust large and powerful organizations. The lone employee who risks his or her job in order to bring abuses and wrongdoing to light has taken on the status of a hero.
Indeed, such disclosures often play an important role in maintaining integrity and efficiency in business and government. However, Mr. Speaker, 1 find I must strongly oppose this motion. For no matter how commendable may be the sentiment that inspired it, it is seriously flawed because it is too sweeping, too general, and too vague, and because it fails to take into account a great many realities and factors in the areas of labour law and of employer-employee relations.
In short, it seems to me that the full repercussions of these proposed measures have not been sufficiently identified. Or considered. In the first place, human nature being as it is, it is obvious that not all disclosures are necessarily motivated by high ideals. Frivolous disclosures inspired by reasons other than commitment to the public good can and do occur, and may well be in nobody's best interest.
Mr. Speaker, when we examine this motion in detail rather than dwelling on the overall principle that inspired it, its flaws become clearly evident. For instance, the motion mentions disclosure of "mismanagement", as well as disclosure of legal violations. Now, Mr. Speaker, a legal violation may be determined by referring to definitions contained in law. But what exactly is mismanagement? When does a waste of funds become "gross"? What exactly is an abuse of authority? One person's mismanagement is another's reasonable decision. What one person sees as an abuse of authority may appear as firm, decisive action to another.
This brings me, Mr. Speaker, to another serious problem with this resolution. It is proposed that employees who make such disclosures shall enjoy protection "unless the employee knows that the report is false." Who would bear the onus of proving that the employee knew the report was false? Could any employee who wishes to discredit an employer avail himself of this provision? In many cases, disclosures may be based on half-truths and partial information. The employee may happen to see a document proposing a course of action that would in fact have been illegal but which, unknown to the employee, had been rejected in a subsequent decision. Could such an employee not honestly claim that he did not know his report was false? If the employee's disclosures were reported in the media, subsequent corrections and retractions would, in fact, do little to repair the damage caused by the initial publicity. Which brings me, Mr. Speaker, to an unjustified assumption upon which this entire motion seems based, namely, that the media will in all cases accurately assess the credibility of a disclosure and report the pertinent facts in a just and even-handed manner, and that the significance of a particular fact or event will be reported in context.

March 27, 1987
Public Service
It should also be noted, Mr. Speaker, that the proposed measure could lead to serious problems for employees as well. Employees who unknowingly cause a false report to be published in the media might be protected from dismissal, but they would not necessarily be protected from a libel action by employers.
The provisions of this motion would affect roughly 900,000 persons in the federal Public Service, and in industries and Crown corporations regulated by the Canada Labour Code, but would also apply to "employees of businesses contracting with the federal Government".
Also, Mr. Speaker, since the provinces have jurisdiction over labour law in most enterprises in Canada, it can safely be assumed that many or most of the businesses contracting with the federal Government are under provincial labour jurisdiction, including construction firms, almost all forms of manufacturing, and many forms of service industry. Yet, according to the terms of this motion, the Parliament of Canada would be assuming the right to regulate an aspect of employer-employee relationships within these enterprises. For this reason, Mr. Speaker, I have serious misgivings as to whether this particular provision of the motion, if enacted, would even be constitutional.
In respect to labour relations, this motion ignores another important reality, namely, the privacy of the collective bargaining system as a preferred and viable way to achieve realistic solutions to workplace problems. Intrinsic to this principle is the fact that group rights, with certain caveats, take precedence over individual rights. This means that the locus of responsibility for workplace problems primarly rests with the duly elected representatives of workers-union officials. These officials are expected to, and in fact are required to-pursuant to the duty of fair representation requirements of Section 136.1 of part V-act faithfully and fairly on behalf of the employees they represent.
This would clearly include a responsibility to respond to the kinds of problems detailed in the Hon. Member's motion. It would not necessarily, however, involve a rather kneejerk public disclosure of the alleged problem. This is so because the collective bargaining system rightfully recognizes that with few exceptions the most meaningful forum within which to address and resolve such problems is either the bargaining table during the open period of collective agreements or by ongoing dialogues with management during the term of agreements. It should be stressed that disputes arising during the term of agreements can, where impasses occur, be resolved through the grievance/arbitration system, as the previous speaker said.
Mr. Speaker, this motion, when examined in detail, proves to be ill-conceived, vague, overly general, and basically
counter-productive. That is why I urge this House to vote against its adoption.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate on a motion introduced by the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway), a member for whom I have a great deal of respect.
This matter was given a thorough airing in this Chamber only some six weeks ago, on the second reading of a Bill which was introduced by another colleague, the Hon. Member for Hastings-Frontenac-Lennox and Addington (Mr. Van-koughnet). The Bill was aimed at providing sanctions to help prevent public sector employers from discharging employees in retaliation for reporting, or blowing the whistle, on serious misconduct by their employers. Bill C-229 called for amendments to the Canada Labour Code, the Canadian Human Rights Act, and the Public Service Employment Act.
The motion we are debating today, if adopted, would have the Government consider the advisability of introducing legislation to protect a wide range of employees, including those in the federal Public Service, Crown corporations, the transportation and communications sectors, and those employees of companies which contract with the federal Government. As you will appreciate, this is a huge number of people, so huge that I dare say no Member of the House, and certainly not myself, could tell you today what that number is.
These people would be employees of organizations that are very different in size and mandate. They vary enormously also in the amount of influence they might have on the daily lives of ordinary Canadians. At one end of the spectrum we would have the federal Public Service, the largest employer in Canada, with approximately 230,000 employees across the country. At the other end, we could conceivably have small businesses, perhaps consisting of no more than a few employees. The motion proposes that these people be afforded special protection from a variety of sanctions when they report on such things as perceived violations of the law, alleged mismanagement, possible gross waste of funds, or abuses of authority.

I would like to look back for a moment to Bill C-229. Its purpose was to provide sanctions for those who might retaliate against whistleblowers. As one way of looking at these two approaches, we might say that one could take a punitive approach, and as the other, a protective approach. It would seem to me that the latter, the protective approach, would be more in keeping with modern human resource management if, indeed, new protective measures are actually warranted.
March 27, 1987

Bill C-229 proposed amendments to legislation. This motion, on the other hand, envisages a new piece of legislation. No one needs to be reminded that Acts of Parliament have a habit of spawning regulations, regulations spawn policies, and policies lead to directives, which in turn call for interpretation, updates, monitoring and administration until, inevitably, they spawn their own bureaucracy to oversee everything.
During the debate in this Chamber in January on Bill C-229, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State made what I think is a very important point in relation to the experience to date since the Civil Service Reform Act was passed in the United States in 1978. This U.S. Act provides protections such as those envisaged in Bill C-229. The Parliamentary Secretary made his point in the form of a question, and I think that question is crucial to the debate on this motion as well. He asked: "What are the motives of the whistleblowers?" This nagging question has been asked many times in the United States since the passage of its protective legislation. I think Hon. Members must ask themselves that question before we proceed further in our review of this motion.
Authorities on the whistleblowing phenomenon have noted that whistleblowing can be a defensive mechanism on the part of employees who are already under threat of disciplinary action for reasons unrelated to the alleged misconduct. In other words, public servants about to be discharged for unsatisfactory work performance could seek to protect themselves by accusing superior officers of misconduct. Whistleblowing can also result from personal or organizational conflicts, again unrelated to the alleged misconduct complained of. What about employees using this blanket protection to embarrass the Government of the day for personal partisan political reasons? It seems to me that the potential for abuse is very significant.
Hon. Members will see from these serious concerns just what a complex issue this is. Its very complexity is reflected in the infinite variety of circumstances in each instance, affecting and influencing the actions of each individual whistleblower. What of those who blow the whistle using proper existing internal procedures, alerting superior officers or senior management so that appropriate action can be taken? I think it is clear that it is virtually impossible to subject all these organizations, all their people and all circumstances to the rule of rigid law and regulations, rigidly prescribed and rigidly enforced.
Hon. Members will know that there is already in place legislation which deals with the abuse of authority and responsibility by public servants at all levels. Section 110(1) (c) of the Criminal Code, for instance, makes it an offence for any official or employee of the Public Service to demand, accept or offer, or to agree to accept from a person dealing with the Government, any reward, advantage or benefit, either directly or indirectly, through anyone else, for his or her own benefit without appropriate authorization. There are sanctions in place now to prevent, avert or penalize proven dishonourable
Public Service
conduct, criminal actions, waste, extravagance, discrimination or abuse of trust.
Standards of conduct have been in place since 1973 and many departments have their codes of discipline to deal with misconduct. There is, as you know, Mr. Speaker, a code of conduct and conflict of interest guidelines for public servants, much like those which apply to elected public office holders. Parliament has already seen fit to pass legislation in the context of the federal Public Service which is designed to prevent abuses and protect employees. The Public Service Staff Relations Act is a good example. It applies to about 200,000 public service employees.
That Act allows employees to grieve any perceived injustice or wrongdoing where there is no other recourse provided in law. In some cases, employees may bring their grievances before an independent third party, or even before the courts.
No amount of legislation will prevent some managers from doing what others may call or classify as "wrongdoing". The best that good internal management and legislation can offer is to present the mechanism and opportunity for fair and adequate recourse for the offended party, all the way to an independent third party, if need be. Existing legislation does that now. The Canadian Human Rights Act protects employees from discrimination. The Privacy Act provides a measure of protection as well.
Returning to the Public Service, the personal harassment policy adopted by Treasury Board for all Public Service employees, specifically forbids harassment for any reason whatsoever. It provides a simple and confidential mechanism which allows employees to bring their concerns to the attention of a neutral third party.
The Public Service Commission which is, of course, an independent agency of Parliament, has a staff of investigators who look into cases of impropriety brought to their attention. The Public Service Employment Act provides for a quasijudicial tribunal known as an appeal board, which is empowered to make rulings on alleged irregularities in connection with the staffing process. The Public Service Commission also has certain powers under the Inquiries Act to investigate allegations of fraud.
Another independent agency of Parliament, the Office of the Auditor General of Canada, has a proven track record of uncovering examples of mismanagement or even fraud. Most departments, in addition, now have in place an effective internal audit mechanism which can advise senior management on these matters.
Any debate on the issue of mismanagement or abuse of power cannot overlook the power of the press in Canada or, indeed, of the power of the Public Service employee unions. Both of these bodies have demonstrated a continuing interest in keeping government employees and public sector organizations, inside the Public Service and beyond, on the straight and narrow, and they have done a very good job indeed.

March 27, 1987
Public Service
I respect the Hon. Member's motives in introducing this motion. It is an important and difficult issue, worthy of debate and further discussion. I am a former public servant myself, indeed, I am the only public servant who was elected in the last election. When I joined the Public Service I took an oath of allegiance to Her Majesty, the Queen. I took an oath of secrecy as well. That always meant something to me as a public servant and I think it means a good deal to most public servants. An oath is something which is just that, something sacred and important to all good citizens.
It seems to me that this motion in its present form would undermine the basic obligation to the Crown which all public servants have and the obligation to an employer which any good and dutiful employee has to that employer. There may
well be room, from my own point of view, for consideration of whistleblower legislation for a narrow area of public policy. I think particularly of serious environmental dangers or hazards to public health or safety. However, this motion, in my view, is too wide and simply too open to abuse.
